name: Excel and Spreadsheets for Work
objectives: In a blank Excel or Google Sheets file, enter a small table with headers in row 1 and one record in each row, with one kind of data per column
Given a table of data, format the headers in bold, money as currency and columns to fit, so it reads clearly at a glance
Given a column of numbers, write SUM, AVERAGE and row formulas and copy them down with the fill handle, with correct results and no error messages
Given a rule such as a sales goal or 40 hours, write an IF formula that labels each row, with the right label on every row
Given a table of at least 8 rows, sort the whole table, add a filter and freeze the header row, without mixing up any rows
Given labels and numbers, make a column chart and share the file with the lowest access the person needs, with no private information in the shared sheet

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Cells, rows, columns and entering data
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Open a new spreadsheet and enter a small table of data with headers.
This lesson builds toward: In a blank Excel or Google Sheets file, you will enter a small table with headers in row 1 and one record in each row, with one kind of data per column.
A spreadsheet is a grid. Columns run up and down and have letters (A, B, C). Rows run across and have numbers (1, 2, 3). Each box is a cell, named by its column and row: the top-left cell is A1. A file can hold several sheets, shown as tabs at the bottom.
To enter data, click a cell, type, and press Enter to move down or Tab to move right. Put headers in row 1, such as Date, Item, Quantity and Price, and one record in each row below. Keep one kind of data per column: only dates in the Date column, only numbers in Price.
To fix a cell, click it and type over it, or double-click to edit part of it. Undo (Ctrl+Z on Windows, Cmd+Z on a Mac) takes back your last change. Excel on the web and Google Sheets save as you work; in desktop Excel, save often.
To start: in Google Sheets, go to sheets.google.com and choose a blank spreadsheet. In Excel, open Excel (or Excel on the web at office.com) and choose a blank workbook.
Step by step:
- Open a blank spreadsheet in Google Sheets or Excel.
- Click cell A1 and type your first header. Press Tab to move right.
- Type the other headers in row 1.
- Enter one record per row starting in row 2.
- Give the file a clear name, such as "Weekly Sales - March".
Words to know:
- Cell: one box in the grid, named by column letter and row number, like B3.
- Header: the label at the top of a column that says what is in it.
- Workbook: an Excel file; it can hold several sheets.
Try it now: Open a blank spreadsheet. In row 1 type the headers Day, Item, Quantity, Price. Enter 8 rows of practice sales (for example Mon, Coffee, 12, 3.50). Name the file "Practice Sales".
You can now open a spreadsheet, find any cell by its name, and enter a clean table with headers.

options: A tab at the bottom of the file
One box in the grid, named by its column and row
check.why: Each box in the grid is a cell, named by its column letter and row number, such as A1.

check.q: You are making a price list. What goes in the Price column?
options: Prices and item names mixed together
Prices and notes about each customer
check.why: Keep one kind of data per column, so the Price column holds only numbers.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Formatting so it is easy to read
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Format headers, money and column widths so the sheet is clear.
This lesson builds toward: Given a table of data, you will format the headers in bold, money as currency and columns to fit, so it reads clearly at a glance.
Formatting changes how data looks, not what it is. Good formatting makes a sheet easy to read at a glance.
Make headers bold: select row 1 and click the B (Bold) button on the toolbar, or press Ctrl+B (Cmd+B on a Mac). You can also add a fill color to the header row.
Show money as currency: select the Price column, then open the number format menu and choose Currency. In Excel this is on the Home tab; in Google Sheets it is under Format, then Number, and there is also a $ button on the toolbar.
Make columns fit: double-click the line between two column letters at the top, and the column on the left resizes to fit its longest entry. This works in both Excel and Google Sheets.
Step by step:
- Select row 1 by clicking the number 1 at the left.
- Click Bold (B) or press Ctrl+B.
- Select the Price column by clicking its letter.
- Choose Currency from the number format menu (Excel: Home tab; Sheets: Format > Number, or the $ button).
- Double-click the border between column letters to auto-fit the width.
Words to know:
- Formatting: changing how data looks (bold, color, currency) without changing the value.
- Select: click or drag over cells to choose them before you act on them.
Try it now: In your Practice Sales sheet, make row 1 bold with a light fill color, show the Price column as currency, and auto-fit every column.
You can now format headers, money and column widths so a sheet is clear and professional.

options: How the data looks, not what it is
check.why: Formatting changes how data looks, such as bold or currency, not its value.

check.q: A column is too narrow and cuts off the text. What do you do?
options: Retype the text in two cells
Double-click the line between the column letters at the top
check.why: Double-clicking the border resizes the column to fit its longest entry.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Totals and averages with SUM and AVERAGE
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write SUM and AVERAGE formulas and copy a formula down a column.
This lesson builds toward: Given a column of numbers, you will write SUM, AVERAGE and row formulas and copy them down with the fill handle, with correct results and no error messages.
A formula always starts with an equals sign (=). It can do math with cell names: =C2*D2 multiplies the quantity in C2 by the price in D2. If you change C2, the answer updates by itself.
SUM adds a range of cells. A range is written as first cell, colon, last cell: =SUM(E2:E9) adds E2 through E9. AVERAGE finds the average: =AVERAGE(E2:E9). Both work the same way in Excel and Google Sheets.
To copy a formula down a column, click the cell with the formula, then drag the small square at its bottom-right corner (the fill handle) down. The cell names change for each row: E2 becomes E3, E4 and so on.
Check your work: if a formula shows an error such as #NAME? or #VALUE!, look for a typo in the function name or text in a number column.
Step by step:
- In E1 type the header Total.
- In E2 type =C2*D2 and press Enter.
- Drag the fill handle from E2 down to the last row.
- Below the last row, type =SUM(E2:E9) for the grand total.
- Under that, type =AVERAGE(E2:E9) for the average sale.
Words to know:
- Formula: a calculation in a cell that starts with = and updates when the data changes.
- Range: a block of cells written first:last, like E2:E9.
- Fill handle: the small square at the bottom-right of a selected cell that you drag to copy.
Try it now: In your sheet, add a Total column with =C2*D2 copied down, then add a grand total with SUM and the average sale with AVERAGE under the column. Change one quantity and watch the totals update.
You can now write SUM and AVERAGE formulas, multiply cells, and copy a formula down a column.

options: Multiplies the value in C2 by the value in D2
check.why: The * sign multiplies, so =C2*D2 multiplies quantity by price.

check.q: You need the total of E2 through E9. What do you type?
check.why: SUM adds a range written as first cell, colon, last cell, and every formula starts with =.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Making decisions with IF
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write an IF formula that labels each row based on a rule.
This lesson builds toward: Given a rule such as a sales goal or 40 hours, you will write an IF formula that labels each row, with the right label on every row.
IF checks a condition and shows one result if it is true and another if it is false. The pattern is =IF(test, value if true, value if false).
Examples: =IF(E2>=50,"Goal met","Below goal") labels a sale. =IF(C2>40,"Overtime","Regular") labels a week of hours. =IF(D2="","Missing","OK") flags an empty cell. Text answers go inside double quotes; numbers do not.
Comparison signs: > greater than, < less than, >= greater than or equal to, <= less than or equal to, = equal to, <> not equal to.
IF works the same in Excel and Google Sheets. If your sheet's region setting uses commas for decimals, the separator may be a semicolon (;) instead of a comma; the app will show you the pattern as you type.
Step by step:
- Add a header, such as Status, to the next empty column.
- In row 2 type =IF(
- Type the test, such as E2>=50, then a comma.
- Type the true result in quotes, a comma, the false result in quotes, and ).
- Press Enter and copy the formula down with the fill handle.
Words to know:
- IF: a function that shows one result when a test is true and another when it is false.
- Condition: the test in an IF formula, such as E2>=50.
Try it now: Add a Status column to your sheet with =IF(E2>=50,"Goal met","Below goal") and copy it down. Change one total so it crosses 50 and watch the label change.
You can now write an IF formula that labels rows automatically based on a rule.

check.q: What does the IF function do?
options: Shows one result if a test is true and another if it is false
check.why: The pattern is =IF(test, value if true, value if false).

check.q: You want to label sales of 50 or more as "Goal met". Which formula do you type in row 2?
check.why: The test E2>=50 comes first, and text results go inside double quotes.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Sorting, filtering and freezing the header row
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort your data, filter it to show only some rows, and freeze the header row.
This lesson builds toward: Given a table of at least 8 rows, you will sort the whole table, add a filter and freeze the header row, without mixing up any rows.
Sorting puts rows in order, such as highest sale first or names A to Z. Filtering hides rows you do not need right now, such as showing only "Below goal" rows. Neither deletes any data.
Excel: click any cell in your table, go to the Data tab, and choose Sort to pick a column and an order, or choose Filter to add drop-down arrows to the header row. Google Sheets: select your data, open the Data menu and choose Sort range (tick that the data has a header row), or choose Create a filter to add the arrows. Click an arrow in a header to sort or to tick only the values you want to see.
Always sort the whole table, not one column alone, or rows get mixed up. Selecting one cell inside the table in Excel, or the full range in Sheets, keeps rows together.
Freezing keeps the header row on screen when you scroll down a long list. Excel: View tab, Freeze Panes, then Freeze Top Row. Google Sheets: View menu, Freeze, then 1 row.
Step by step:
- Click inside your table (Excel) or select the whole table (Sheets).
- Sort: Excel Data tab > Sort; Sheets Data > Sort range, with a header row.
- Filter: Excel Data tab > Filter; Sheets Data > Create a filter.
- Use the arrow in a header to show only the rows you want.
- Freeze: Excel View > Freeze Panes > Freeze Top Row; Sheets View > Freeze > 1 row.
Words to know:
- Sort: put rows in order by one column, keeping each row together.
- Filter: hide rows that do not match what you choose, without deleting them.
- Freeze: keep rows or columns on screen while you scroll.
Try it now: Sort your sheet by Total from largest to smallest. Add a filter and show only "Below goal" rows, then clear the filter. Freeze the top row and scroll down to check the headers stay.
You can now sort and filter data safely and freeze the header row.

check.q: What does freezing the header row do?
options: Locks the file so no one can edit
Keeps the header row on screen when you scroll down
check.why: Freezing keeps the header visible while you scroll through a long list.

check.q: You want to see only the "Below goal" rows for now, without losing any data. What do you use?
options: A filter on the header row
check.why: A filter hides the rows you do not need right now and deletes nothing.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Making a chart and sharing your sheet
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a simple column chart and share the sheet with the right permission.
This lesson builds toward: Given labels and numbers, you will make a column chart and share the file with the lowest access the person needs, with no private information in the shared sheet.
A chart turns numbers into a picture. A column chart is good for comparing amounts, such as sales by day or volunteer hours by person.
Select two columns: the labels (such as Day) and the numbers (such as Total), including the headers. To select two columns that are not next to each other, hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) while you select the second one. Excel: go to the Insert tab and choose a column chart (or Recommended Charts). Google Sheets: open the Insert menu and choose Chart; the chart editor opens on the right, where you can pick Column chart. Click the chart title to rename it.
To share: in Google Sheets, click the Share button at the top right, type the person's email, and choose Viewer, Commenter or Editor. In Excel, the file must be saved to OneDrive or SharePoint; then click Share, add the email, and choose whether they can edit or only view.
Share safely: give the lowest access the person needs (view-only if they just need to read it), and never put passwords, Social Security numbers or bank details in a shared sheet.
Step by step:
- Select the label column and the number column, with headers.
- Excel: Insert tab > a column chart. Sheets: Insert > Chart, then choose Column chart.
- Rename the chart title.
- Click Share, add the person's email.
- Choose view-only unless they need to edit, then send.
Words to know:
- Column chart: a chart with bars standing up, good for comparing amounts.
- Viewer: someone who can see a shared file but not change it.
- Editor: someone who can change a shared file.
Try it now: Final task: finish your sheet with at least 8 rows, bold headers, currency, SUM and AVERAGE, an IF Status column, sorted highest to lowest, a filter, a column chart of Day and Total, and the top row frozen. Then share it with one person as a viewer.
You can now make a column chart from your data and share a spreadsheet with the right permission.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clean data table Fewer than 8 rows, missing headers, or mixed data in a column. Headers in row 1, at least 8 rows, one kind of data per column. The file and sheet tab have clear names. Easy to read Headers are plain, money has no currency format, or text is cut off. Headers in bold, money shown as currency, columns fit their entries. The header row also has a fill color and the sheet looks tidy. Totals and average Totals typed by hand or a formula shows an error. A SUM total and an AVERAGE that give the right results. Row totals use a formula copied down with the fill handle. IF labels No IF column, or labels are wrong. An IF column labels every row correctly, such as "Goal met" or "Below goal". Can explain the test and change the goal number to update the labels. Sorted, filtered and frozen Rows are mixed up, or the sort, filter or freeze is missing. Data sorted highest to lowest, a filter on the header row, and the top row frozen. Can use the filter to show only one label and then clear it. Chart and safe sharing No chart, or shared with edit access by default or with private data. A titled column chart, and the file shared with one person as a viewer, with no private data. Can say why they chose that access level. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which chart is good for comparing amounts, such as hours by person?
check.why: The lesson says a column chart is good for comparing amounts.

check.q: Your manager only needs to read your sheet. Which access do you give when you share it?
options: Anyone with the link can edit
check.why: Give the lowest access the person needs; view-only if they just need to read it.
